core_condition: at least one measured effect recorded in observed_effects from Ventora telemetry or public corpora

evidence.rationale: Four decades of convergent work. Baddeley & Hitch (1974) established the working-memory constraint; Sweller (1988) demonstrated that problem-solving formats consuming that capacity impair learning; Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas (1998) set out the architecture; Chandler & Sweller (1991) established the split-attention effect; Sweller et al. (2019) reviewed twenty further years. The corpus contains all of these plus Paas's measurement work and Ginns's contiguity meta-analysis. The core empirical claim — that load imposed by presentation rather than by the task degrades comprehension — is among the best-supported findings in instructional psychology.

product_applicability.rationale: Directly implementable and cross-cutting: extraneous-element reduction, chunking and progressive disclosure, split-attention avoidance apply to every artifact type from landing to checkout. Reference at scale: Stripe Checkout's sequenced fields, search-result sparseness, progressive-disclosure product pages.

measurability.rationale: Proxies are directly reachable by our telemetry: task_completion_rate, time_to_complete, error_rate, drop_off_by_step, form_completion. Load itself is measured in the literature mainly by subjective scales, but we do not need to measure load — we measure the performance consequences it predicts.

orthogonality.rationale: CL-14 is the capacity constraint underlying much of S7: MM-15 is largely applied load management, PF-16 correlates with load, SC-17's scanning is partly an adaptation to it. Retained as a distinct L1 because chunking, progressive disclosure and split-attention avoidance are implementations belonging to the constraint itself rather than to any of the others. Score 2 reflects real, documented overlap within the node.

safety.rationale: Reducing extraneous load is user-serving by construction. Two misuse vectors exist and are blocked: deliberately raising load to obstruct an action (confusing cancellation flows, deliberately dense terms — an EU/FTC dark-pattern target), and 'simplification' that removes material information the user needs. Both are hard rules; the boundary is clear and testable.

dissent: Three substantive critiques are on record and shape how we claim this. (1) Measurement: cognitive load is largely assessed by subjective self-report scales; the construct validity of these measures has been repeatedly questioned, which weakens quantitative claims about how much load a given design imposes — hence we claim direction, not magnitude. (2) The germane-load construct has been criticised as difficult to falsify and partly circular within the theory, prompting its revision in later formulations; our claims rest on the intrinsic/extraneous distinction, which is the empirically load-bearing part. (3) Expertise reversal: presentation that reduces load for novices can impair experienced users, for whom redundant scaffolding becomes extraneous itself — so 'less' is not universally better, it is better relative to the user's prior knowledge. A fourth boundary is ours rather than the literature's: the evidence base is overwhelmingly instructional (learning outcomes in educational settings), not commercial interfaces measured on conversion and retention. The transfer is plausible and is why the mechanism enters as incubating rather than core, but it is a transfer, and our own measurement is what should confirm it.
